summary.zh: Leiber和Stoller将R&B、古典弦乐和拉丁节奏进行融合，创作出了Sweet Soul风格。

body.zh:
Leiber和Stoller将R&B、古典弦乐和拉丁节奏进行融合，创作出了Sweet Soul风格。

有人认为1960至1963年是摇滚乐的黄金时期，他们认为Phil Spector是一位天才制作人，能在录音棚中创造出比任何现场表演更好的音效，把录音棚当做乐器，并把这一创举看作音乐产业中不可思议的进步。说英伦入侵打断了这个黄金期并不公平，因为就算当Brian Wilson和The Beatles进入录音棚时，他们也想以Phil Spector的成就为基础，某种意义上是Phil Spector的学生和追随者。

但是有人说另一种风格由于英伦入侵而被削弱了，那就是Sweet Soul。它是一种优秀的非裔美国人音乐，花了很长时间才打入流行榜单，复杂且精妙。当英国人梳着个性的头发，穿着酷炫的西装，夹杂着口音，身背吉他在台上热情洋溢地演唱《She Loves You》和《I Want to Hold Your Hand》的时候，他们的表演形式比很多Sweet Soul歌手更粗糙。当然，你对此可以有自己的观点。

Sweet Soul大约源自Nat King Cole和Johnny Mathis这些黑人艺人，主题往往是成年人的浪漫而非少年题材，例如Nat King Cole在1958年的《Looking Back》、Johnny Mathis在1957年的《Chances Are》和1959年的《Misty》，都是优美的情歌，有当年Frank Sinatra和Dean Martin的风范，但没有big band（大型爵士乐队）为之配乐，取而代之的是管弦乐团的陪衬。

另一个人则是Sam Cooke，他最初演唱Gospel，后来转型为流行歌手，对此他内心相当矛盾，也让他充满了争议。但Sam Cooke的确完成了转型，1957年他拥有了一支冠军单曲《You Send Me》，直到60年代早期，他的歌曲都持续被主流榜单认可，1963年的《Another Saturday Night》位列榜单第九名。但悲剧的是，他在1964年死于谋杀，好像是为某位女性在汽车旅馆与人发生了口角，我不太清楚。在那段时间里，很多事情都蒙上了神秘的面纱，他去世时实在太年轻，但嗓音极佳，是Sweet Soul的先驱。

Sweet Soul真正形成流派，是在Leiber和Stoller开始熟悉它，并把R&B、古典弦乐和拉丁节奏融为一体之后。第一首成功实践该融合的歌曲是1959年The Drifters的亚军单曲《There Goes My Baby》。当Leiber和Stoller把《There Goes My Baby》带给在Atlantic Records负责演出事务的Jerry Wexler时，Wexler并不打算发行这支单曲。这首歌里的R&B听起来带有些Doo-wop的味道，从中还能发现古典乐的影子，而且不仅是古典弦乐，夹杂在音符之间的旋律听起来又像出自19世纪末的俄罗斯民族主义音乐家Mussorgsky、Borodin或Tchaikovsky之手。他觉得这么迥异的两种风格混在一起，没人会喜欢。所以他说了一句有名的话，《There Goes My Baby》听起来就像收音机卡在了两个频道中间，一边是古典乐频道，另一边则是R&B。但Leiber和Stoller坚持要发行，事实证明他们是对的，这首歌不仅为The Drifters带来荣耀，而且开启了乐队主唱Ben E. King的音乐事业。

学习摇滚史的过程中，你可能看到音乐人越来越野心勃勃，越来越想做更大胆、更好的音乐，他们开始不满足于把流行乐看做一次性商品，而是想创造更多具有长远价值的音乐。在《There Goes My Baby》中，你就能看到这种野心的开端。在接下来的几章里，当我们讨论60、70、80年代的摇滚乐时，会继续跟进这个话题。

在《There Goes My Baby》大热后，Ben E. King在The Drifters中演唱了一段时间，然后退团单飞了，Rudy Lewis取代了他。所以Leiber和Stoller同时与Ben E. King和The Drifters合作：与Ben E King合作时，《Spanish Harlem》位列1961年榜单第十，《Stand By Me》位列1961年第四，两首歌都带有拉丁风味。与The Drifters（Rudy Lewis担任主唱）合作时，《Up On the Roof》位列1962年榜单第五名，《On Broadway》则位列1963年榜单第九

如我所言，如果你是该时期的拥护者，或许是因为你觉得混合R&B、古典和拉丁元素的Sweet Soul是一种精妙的音乐形式，被低估但令人印象深刻。
body.en:
Leiber and Stoller fuse R&B, classical strings, and Latin rhythm into what becomes Sweet Soul.

Some call 1960–1963 rock’s golden stretch: Phil Spector as genius, making studio results better than any stage, treating the studio as an instrument—an astonishing industrial advance. It is unfair to say the British Invasion simply breaks that golden run; when Brian Wilson and the Beatles enter the studio they build on Spector—in a sense they are his students and heirs.

Others say Sweet Soul is the style the Invasion weakens. It is fine African American music, slow to crack the pop charts, complex and subtle. When Brits with distinctive hair, sharp suits, accents, and guitars belting “She Loves You” and “I Want to Hold Your Hand,” their presentation is rougher than many Sweet Soul singers. You can hold your own view.

Sweet Soul roughly descends from Black artists such as Nat King Cole and Johnny Mathis—adult romance more than teen themes: Cole’s 1958 “Looking Back,” Mathis’s 1957 “Chances Are” and 1959 “Misty”—elegant love songs in a Sinatra/Dean Martin vein, but with orchestra instead of big band.

Then Sam Cooke: from gospel into pop, conflicted and controversial about the turn, yet he makes it—1957’s No. 1 “You Send Me,” mainstream recognition into the early 1960s, 1963’s “Another Saturday Night” at No. 9. Tragically he is murdered in 1964—apparently a motel quarrel over a woman; details stay murky. He dies very young with a superb voice; a Sweet Soul pioneer.

Sweet Soul coheres as a style once Leiber and Stoller learn it and fuse R&B, classical strings, and Latin rhythm. The first successful practice is the Drifters’ 1959 No. 2 “There Goes My Baby.” When they bring it to Atlantic’s Jerry Wexler, he does not want to release it: R&B with doo-wop flavor plus classical shadows—not only strings, but melodic turns that sound like late-19th-century Russian nationalists (Mussorgsky, Borodin, Tchaikovsky). He thinks nobody will like such a clash. His famous line: it sounds like a radio stuck between classical and R&B. Leiber and Stoller insist; they are right—the record elevates the Drifters and launches lead Ben E. King’s career.

Across rock history you will see musicians grow more ambitious—wanting bolder, better music, not disposable pop but work with lasting value. “There Goes My Baby” shows that ambition starting. Later chapters on the 1960s–80s will keep that thread.

After the hit, Ben E. King stays with the Drifters a while, then goes solo; Rudy Lewis replaces him. Leiber and Stoller work both sides: with King, 1961’s “Spanish Harlem” (No. 10) and “Stand by Me” (No. 4), both with Latin flavor; with the Drifters (Lewis on lead), 1962’s “Up on the Roof” (No. 5) and 1963’s “On Broadway” (No. 9).

As I said: if you defend this period, it may be because Sweet Soul’s R&B–classical–Latin mix feels subtle, underrated, and impressive.
